extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for classroom management, moral instruction, and composition exercises in primary/elementary schools, including topics for pupil writing, group exercises, and procedures for handling individual offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use composition/moral exercises to produce moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary operation of composition exercises is calculated to produce moral effect among pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign descriptive and reflective exercises (e.g., first impressions, personal anecdotes) and read/comment on many such pieces to influence sentiment and character; examples in the chapter are offered as specimens rather than exceptional compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to parents (essay subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign topics involving 'DUTIES TO PARENTS' such as anecdotes of good or bad conduct at home, questions, cases of difficulty in obeying, dialogues between parents and children, and excuses for disobedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning the subject, give suggestions about the kinds of articles pupils may write (anecdotes, dialogues, questions) so that essays focus on concrete instances and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selfishness (essay subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign 'SELFISHNESS' as a topic: cases of selfishness observed, dialogues exhibiting it, questions about its nature, and indications of selfish behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage pupils to draw on observed incidents and dialogues to analyze the nature and signs of selfishness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faults of the school (essay subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign 'FAULTS OF THE SCHOOL': pupils report bad practices observed in deportment, recitations, study habits, treatment of one another; write on their greatest trouble and possible remedies; suggest improvements in management without naming individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these writings to gather candid feedback and to identify manageable changes in school administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellences of the school (essay subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign 'EXCELLENCES OF THE SCHOOL': pupils note good practices to persevere, incidents illustrating good character, cases of right action under temptation, and favorable community reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforce positive habits by having pupils describe and praise exemplary conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sabbath (essay subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign 'THE SABBATH': have pupils describe doubtful practices observed on the Sabbath, questions and differing opinions they have heard, and difficulties in proper Sabbath observance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the topic to surface pupils' uncertainties and to encourage moral reasoning about leisure and observance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide anonymous school writing channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a place of deposit for anonymous writings to be read in school, allowing teachers and pupils to contribute without attaching names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions like a school newspaper: sentiments and opinions influence according to intrinsic merit, free from name-based prejudice; the teacher should sometimes submit anonymous pieces to guide discussion; allow full discussions, criticisms of management, good-humored satires, and descriptions—limit time (e.g., 15 minutes) for reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher editorial control over anonymous submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher must have the usual editorial powers to comment upon, alter, or suppress anonymous writings as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial discretion to prevent harm, shape moral lessons, and maintain order while encouraging free expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize 'marks of a bad scholar' (signs to evaluate pupils)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify signs of a 'bad scholar': hurried, ill-humored preparation, inattention at devotional exercises, forgotten or mistaken tasks, hesitation in answers, inattention to general instructions, excuses for reproval, indolence, lazy posture, lingering gait when leaving seat, untidiness of books, scattering waste paper, ink-stained hands and clothes, blotted and mistake-filled written exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to evaluate pupil habits and target interventions; the detailed portrait gives specific behaviors to observe and remediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach punctuality by moral illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Use anecdotes (e.g., steamboat rescue) to illustrate 'THE CONSEQUENCES OF BEING BEHINDHAND' and to teach that habitual tardiness leads to inconvenience and sometimes lasting injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moralize punctuality through vivid stories that make the abstract habit concrete and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage welcoming behavior toward new scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: Combat thoughtless exclusiveness among pupils who fail to make newcomers feel at home; avoid idle discussion of a newcomer's appearance or voice and instead take action to relieve her discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should foster a culture in which current pupils proactively reach out to new pupils; rely on kindness rather than requiring the newcomer to push herself forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage a satirical spirit, allow mild raillery sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemn a 'satirical spirit' that spares neither friend nor foe and wounds others even when the satirist is gifted; however, allow 'a little good-humored raillery' occasionally to attack faults not reachable by graver methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to talents that become instruments of sarcasm; teach the personal cost of biting satire and permit only restrained, good-natured teasing when pedagogically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use variety of activities to secure influence and cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce varied exercises (marching bands, step drills, propositions, compositions with diverse themes) to keep the school engaged: 'how pleasing is variety!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate tunes, recess activities, and composition themes so pupils remain interested; variety helps obtain ascendancy over pupils and build a majority in favor of good order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure the majority through general influences before targeting individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to 'take general views of the condition of the school' and improve it in the mass rather than merely rebuking accidental faults; gain a general influence and ascendancy to control most pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus first on institution-wide habits and morale to bring an 'overwhelming majority' in favor of order; only then address the minority of difficult individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain individual offenders by discreet observation
rubrics_metrics.description: To identify individual offenders, do not appear suspiciously watchful; instead, notice conduct from day to day to understand character without provoking bad behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obvious spying that would invite misbehavior; practice quiet, continuous observation to learn dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore individual character to find reform foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly examine each delinquent's character: find what is good (sources of pride), their peculiar enjoyments, and temptations from home that may explain conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this deeper knowledge to build reforms on existing strengths and to sympathize where appropriate; understanding motives is essential for lasting change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure personal attachment of the pupil to be reformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Gain the personal attachment of the wayward pupil by approaching boldly, manfully, and pleasantly—being superior yet a friend—and by securing the reality of friendship rather than affected smiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask pupils for assistance in small tasks, notice and take an interest in their pursuits, and thus awaken attachment; genuine invitations to help (e.g., cutting quills, arranging papers) often produce reform more effectively than punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor moral remedies over physical punishment when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer moral means (e.g., asking a notorious mischief-maker to help the teacher and thereby experience the pleasure of doing good) to physical punishment, which may breed revenge and further mischief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'whistle' illustration: transforming a boy's skill toward pleasing the master can open new thoughts and attachments that reduce bad behavior; disciplinary measures may still be necessary depending on the offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle deliberate intentional wrong by frank private confrontation
rubrics_metrics.description: When deliberate wrong occurs, calmly think through the case, note palliating circumstances, then go to the individual privately for frank, open dealing: describe the conduct mildly, ask for honest explanation, and request the pupil state whether he will reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it clear that the teacher's duty may require decisive measures, but aim to remove the evil pleasantly; obtain a sincere commitment to reform or an honest admission so future steps are clear. Nine cases out of ten will be resolved by this method.
